title: What is 'community' and why is it important?
author: Toby Lowe
standard: RI.7.2 — determine and summarize the central idea of a text and identify the details that develop it
knowledgeFocus: Defines 'community' as a group of people who share an identity-forming narrative. Used as foundation throughout the unit.
skillFocus: Determining and summarizing the central idea; identifying supporting details.

pacing.activity: Introduce reading lesson and skill focus
Read text and answer DRQs in modalities (whole class, partner, independent)

vocabulary.definition: a feeling of unity or togetherness based on a common interest
the quality that makes something what it is
a part or feature of something
behaving in line with accepted standards

centralIdea: A community is a group of people who share an identity-forming narrative — a story that defines part of who they are, shapes their sense of right and wrong, and lets them be part of multiple communities at once.

textParagraphs.text: The word 'community' has a strange power to it. It conveys a sense of togetherness and positivity. It speaks both of solidarity and homeliness. You will, almost never, hear people say what they mean by 'community'.

Lowe lists what a definition of community must explain: different types (place, dispersed); positive feelings without claiming community is always good (the Mafia is a community); identity and belonging including 'in/out' groups; normative power (shaping what 'good' and 'bad' mean); how it differs from 'society' or 'family'; and that people belong to many communities at once.
Lowe's definition: A community is a group of people who share an identity-forming narrative.
Members build the community's shared story archetypes (characters), history, and lens-on-the-world into their own sense of self.
Lowe's example: he belongs to the Newcastle community. He takes pride in showing the city, feels slighted when people insult it, feels at home hearing a Geordie accent.

What makes him part of Newcastle is the choice to write its stories into his own — friendly, talks to strangers at bus stops, supports Newcastle United, attends shared events at St. James Park, sees the city's future as his own.

Choosing to participate in making and remaking the city's stories is what makes him part of it — not just where he lives or works. People who moved away can still belong; people who live there may not.

Lowe tests his definition against the 6 criteria from paragraph 2. The shared story can be about a place, religion, or social practice; gives positive feelings without being inherently good; explains shared identity through narrative; gives normative force (a 'good neighbor' fits the story we tell); distinguishes community from 'society' or 'family'; and accounts for belonging to multiple communities (and the tensions that creates).
Restated: Community is a group of people who share a story so important to them it defines an aspect of who they are.
Why it matters: a plea for more precise language. Community is one type of grouping that explains shared identity and the lens we see the world through.
Key message: social change requires changing the most important stories we tell ourselves. Social change is change in community.

duringReadingQuestions.question: What claim does Lowe make about the word 'community' in paragraph 1?
duringReadingQuestions.modelAnswer: It is a powerful word that can mean different things, but people aren't always clear what they mean by it.

duringReadingQuestions.question: What is the relationship between the claim and the bulleted list in paragraph 2?
duringReadingQuestions.modelAnswer: Lowe lists what a good definition of community should explain.

duringReadingQuestions.question: Based on the bulleted list, summarize at least three key traits of a community.
How does Lowe's example of belonging to the Newcastle community support his definition?
duringReadingQuestions.modelAnswer: Part of his identity is the shared story of Newcastle — he acts as Geordies are supposed to act, takes pride, and chooses to take part in its events.

duringReadingQuestions.question: Consider the communities you are part of. Share how one fits Lowe's definition.
Why does the author include another bulleted list in paragraph 8?
duringReadingQuestions.modelAnswer: He tests his definition against the six traits from paragraph 2.

duringReadingQuestions.question: Explain at least three reasons why Lowe thinks his 'shared story' definition works.
The title asks 'What is community and why is it important?' Highlight two pieces of evidence that answer both.

multipleChoice.stem: Which best describes the author's main purpose?
choices: A. Show how important multiple communities are
B. Show how community shaped the author's life
C. Describe a Newcastle resident's life
D. Give a clear and useful definition of community

multipleChoice.stem: Which evidence best illustrates the central idea?
choices: C. Para 9 — 'a story that defines an aspect of who they are'

multipleChoice.stem: What is the best meaning of 'slighted' in paragraph 5?
How do paragraphs 5–7 help the reader understand the central idea?
choices: A. Explaining community is neither good nor bad
C. Giving an example of a community in the author's story
D. Showing the diversity of Newcastle

shortResponse.prompt: Explain what Lowe means when he says a community is 'a group of people who share an identity-forming narrative.' Use at least two details from the text and relevant unit vocabulary.
rubricExpectations: Restates Lowe's definition in own words
Two text-based details (e.g., Newcastle example, the 6 criteria)
Uses at least one unit vocabulary word correctly (narrative, aspect, specific, moral)

discussionQuestions: What is something considered courteous behavior in a community you're part of?
Can you be part of a community without conforming to its views?
What might be some benefits of belonging to more than one community?
